title: How greedy and UCB choose
intro: Reading this takes about {minutes} minutes. Read carefully: once you go on, this text closes and you won't see it again. Next you will explain it to Kai, a classmate who missed it, and after that you will solve practice problems and answer a short test, all from memory. So take in as much as you can: how each rule chooses, and why. You don't need to remember UCB's formula; what matters is the idea behind it, what UCB does and in which situations it picks something other than the favourite. Kai learns best from your own words and your own examples, so aim to understand rather than to memorise sentences.

blocks.p: Every day for a year you have lunch at one of three food trucks on campus. Each truck's lunches vary from day to day around a true average quality, which never changes but which you do not know. This is a **multi-armed bandit**: you choose one of several options again and again, each choice gives a random reward, and you want as much reward as possible in total, over all the rounds.

Two things make it hard. You only see the reward of the option you chose: a day at truck A tells you nothing new about B or C. And all you know about a truck is the **average** of the lunches you have had there. An average from two lunches can be far from the truth; an average from fifty is much more reliable, because lucky and unlucky days even out.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. Averages from few and many lunches

blocks.p: A **rule** decides, round after round, which option to pick, using only what has been seen so far: each option's average and how often it was picked. This text explains two rules. Both start by trying every option once, so that each option has an average. The option with the highest average so far is called the **favourite**.
Greedy is the simplest rule: in every round, pick the favourite.

After each round greedy updates the average of the option it picked, and only that one. If the favourite has a poor round, its average drops, and if it drops below another option's average, that option becomes the new favourite and greedy switches to it. Greedy never picks an option just to learn more about it: every pick is the option that looks best right now.

This can go wrong. Since greedy only updates the options it picks, an option whose average falls below the others' is not picked any more, and nothing changes its average after that. This is **lock-in**. Suppose truck A is truly the best, but its first lunch happens to be poor. A's average starts low, greedy picks the other trucks from then on, and it never finds out that A is the best, because it never goes back to check.

Lock-in shows the basic tension of the bandit problem. **Exploiting** means picking the option that looks best, to collect reward now. **Exploring** means picking an option to learn more about it: it may cost reward now, but it can show that an option is better than it looked. Greedy only exploits. Exploring too little risks being stuck with a worse option; exploring too much wastes rounds on options already known to be worse. The next rule, UCB, explores, and it does so on purpose rather than by chance.

sections.title: 3. UCB: the average plus a bonus

blocks.p: UCB ("upper confidence bound") explores in a targeted way, without any randomness. In every round it gives each option a **score** and picks the option with the highest score:

The first term is option i's average and the second is its **bonus**: nᵢ is how often option i has been picked so far, t is the round number, and c is a setting chosen in advance. You will not need to calculate with the formula, but its parts matter.

blocks.caption: Figure 4. One UCB round with three options

blocks.p: Why a bonus? An average from few picks is unreliable: the option's true average could be well above what has been seen so far. Think of a range of plausible values around each average, wide for an option picked a few times and narrow for one picked often. UCB treats every option as if it were as good as it could plausibly be, the top of that range, so options tried only a few times get the benefit of the doubt. That is how it explores: it picks an option when that option might be the best.

How big the bonuses are is set by c, which is chosen in advance to match how much the rewards are expected to vary. With c = 2 every bonus is twice as big as with c = 1, and the averages stay as they are. The bonus does not look at the rewards an option actually gave: it depends only on c, on how often the option was picked and on the round.

The bonus changes in two ways. Each pick of an option makes its own bonus smaller, because its nᵢ grows; picks of other options do not shrink it. And as rounds pass, every bonus grows, because ln(t) grows with t: without limit, but more and more slowly. ln(10) ≈ 2.3, ln(100) ≈ 4.6 and ln(1,000) ≈ 6.9, so each further step of 2.3 takes ten times as many rounds. Only how often an option was picked matters, not when.

blocks.caption: Figure 5. What the bonus depends on

blocks.p: An option that has never been picked has an unlimited bonus, which is why UCB tries every option once first. And there is no randomness: the same history always gives the same pick.
